lesson.title: Coordinates as Keys: Using Tuples in Dictionaries
lesson.summary: Because tuples are immutable and therefore hashable, a tuple can serve as a dictionary key when a single value isn't enough to identify what you're looking up, while a list cannot.
lesson.body:
Dictionaries explained that a dictionary key must be hashable, and Tuple Immutability explained why tuples qualify: once created, a tuple's contents can never change, so Python can compute a stable hash for it and trust that hash forever. Lists fail this requirement for the opposite reason, since a list can be modified after creation, so any hash computed for it could go stale the moment its contents change, and Python refuses to let lists serve as dictionary keys at all.

This distinction matters most when a single value isn't enough to identify what you're looking up. A grid position needs both a row and a column. A geographic coordinate needs both latitude and longitude. Tuples, which group multiple values together into one immutable unit, are a natural fit as dictionary keys in exactly these situations.

distances = {}
distances[(0, 0)] = 0
distances[(1, 2)] = 2.236
distances[(3, 4)] = 5.0

print(distances[(3, 4)])

try:
    distances[[1, 2]] = 5
except TypeError:
    print("Lists cannot be dictionary keys")

print(distances[(3, 4)]) retrieves 5.0, looked up using the tuple (3, 4) as a single, combined key representing an x and y coordinate together. Trying the same thing with a list, [1, 2], instead of a tuple raises a TypeError, since lists are mutable and therefore unhashable, so the except block runs and prints Lists cannot be dictionary keys.

This pattern is common anywhere a lookup naturally depends on more than one piece of information at once: caching the result of a calculation based on two input numbers so it never has to be recomputed, storing which square on a chessboard holds which piece using a (row, column) tuple, or recording a count of how many times each (weekday, hour) combination saw peak website traffic. Any time you catch yourself wanting to combine two or three values into one dictionary key, a tuple is almost always the right tool, precisely because it is immutable in the same way a plain number or string already is.
